The ramp slope must meet building safety guidelines for access.

s.defn: In applied graphs, slope is the rate that one quantity changes compared to another such as distance over time.
ex: Plot speed and time then find the slope as rate of change.
A steep slope on a graph shows a fast increase.

s.defn: To give a surface or line a planned incline measured as vertical rise over horizontal run for drainage or stability.
ex: Engineers slope the walkway to direct rainwater away from the building.
Contractors slope the road shoulder to improve drainage and stability.

s.defn: To incline or descend at an angle or to have a particular gradient, as a line on a graph or a hillside.
ex: The field slopes gently toward the stream so water drains off.
On the graph the line slopes upward as x increases showing positive change.

s.defn: A length of time between two events or marks.

s.defn: In mathematics, the interval is the set of numbers between two endpoints, possibly including the endpoints.

Values lie inside an open interval.

s.defn: The distance in pitch between two tones in music.

A perfect fifth adds harmony to the chord.

s.defn: A short break in a performance or broadcast.
ex: The interval lasted ten minutes.
Audience returns after interval.

s.defn: Relating to or occurring at regular, evenly spaced time intervals.

s.defn: Between two points in a range; intermediate.
ex: An interval value lies between the endpoints of the segment.
An interval measure acts as the mid part of the range.

s.defn: A fundamental truth or proposition that forms the basis for beliefs, decisions, or behavior.
ex: In science, a principle guides the design of experiments.
Honesty is a guiding principle in a daily routine.

s.defn: A rule or guideline used to govern conduct or procedure.
ex: The principle of fair play is taught before group work.
We follow the principle that everyone helps with cleanup.

s.defn: The act of presenting information about events or data to others; giving an account of facts.

Her reporting of the incident kept classmates informed.

s.defn: The process of preparing and presenting a formal written report, especially in business or school settings.
ex: Quarterly reporting requires compiling sales figures.
The classroom project includes progress reporting to teachers.

s.defn: In journalism, the activity of gathering and presenting news information for the public.
ex: Her reporting from the field won a prize.
Reliable reporting relies on official sources.

s.defn: In classroom usage, the act of presenting information, often orally, to a teacher or class as part of an assignment.
ex: Students delivered an oral report to the class.
The lab report shows how to organize findings.

s.defn: To give information about something observed or studied in a formal or organized way.
ex: Students report findings from science experiments to the teacher.
Researchers report results in the class science journal.

s.defn: To present information to a person in charge about a situation or performance, often as a status update.
ex: The class reports to the teacher on weekly science observations.
Staff report to the principal about the incident after it occurs.

s.defn: The act of compiling data and presenting it as a formal document or record.
ex: The student is reporting data in the science lab notebook.
We are reporting the measurements to the class portfolio.

s.defn: Relating to the act of presenting information in reports or to the process of reporting data.
ex: The reporting requirements outline how students present data.
In science class, reporting results helps evidence knowledge.

s.defn: Relating to moral principles and what is right or wrong.

s.defn: Describing actions or decisions that conform to accepted professional standards or codes of conduct.

s.defn: A repair or replacement that restores function to a device, structure, or system.
ex: The quick fix for the broken chair saved the science fair project.
A proper fix requires careful inspection of the mechanism.

s.defn: A difficult situation or predicament in which a person or group must find a solution.
ex: The team faced a tricky fix after the data was lost.

s.defn: To repair something that is broken or damaged so it works again.

Students fixed the leaky faucet in the science room.

s.defn: To fasten or secure something in a fixed position so that it does not move.

We fixed the picture frame to the corkboard.

s.defn: To decide on and arrange in advance such as scheduling a date.
ex: The teacher fixed the date for the field trip.
We fixed the appointment for science lab day.

s.defn: A person who commits a crime, violating criminal law; a person found to have engaged in illegal conduct punishable by the state.

s.defn: A person who violates rules or norms in noncriminal contexts, such as codes of conduct, professional standards, or policy requirements.

Policy violator was disciplined under the university code of conduct.

s.defn: Not awake or responsive; in a state of unconsciousness.

s.defn: Not anticipated or foreseen; not included in prior expectations, particularly in research or analysis, and appearing contrary to hypotheses or forecasts.

s.defn: The breast is the anterior part of the chest in humans, containing the mammary glands and playing a role in lactation.

Mammography assesses breast tissue for tumors.

s.defn: In culinary contexts the breast refers to the front portion of a bird from which edible meat is obtained, especially in poultry.

s.defn: to change something in a planned or partial way, often to improve it or fit a need

s.defn: The person or thing that a text or picture is about or focuses on.
ex: The subject of the biography is a famous scientist.
Discuss the subject of the poem with a partner.

s.defn: To make a person or text undergo an action or treatment, such as a test edit or change.
ex: The teacher may subject a story to revision after group feedback.
Writers can be subjected to peer review in a workshop.

s.defn: To bring a text idea or part of speech under close study or analysis in class.
ex: We will subject the paragraph to close analysis in class.
Students subject sentences to grammar checks during editing.

s.defn: To bring a person group or place under authority or control, often used in historical or literary contexts.
ex: Histories often describe rulers who subject neighboring lands.
The novel shows a character subjected to strict rules at home.

s.defn: Goods taken by victors as prizes after a contest or battle.
ex: The soldiers divided the spoils of war after the battle.
Ancient stories often describe the spoils of conquest as symbols of power.

s.defn: Waste rock or soil removed during mining and not used in the final product.
ex: The spoil from the quarry lay beside the road awaiting disposal.
Engineers used large spoil piles to create a berm around the site.

s.defn: To become rotten or unfit to eat, especially food.
ex: Milk will spoil if left unrefrigerated.
Overripe fruit spoils quickly in heat.

s.defn: To cause something to become worse or less enjoyable; to ruin.
ex: The rain spoiled our picnic plans.
A power outage spoiled the science demonstration.

s.defn: To treat someone, especially a child, with too much kindness or to give in to their wishes.
ex: Grandparents spoil their grandchildren with toys.
Don't spoil him by always saying yes.

s.defn: To reveal a secret or the ending of a story; to spoil.
ex: Don't spoil the ending of the book for us.
Telling the ending would spoil the surprise for the class.

s.defn: Representing things as they actually are, not idealized.
ex: The realistic diagram shows the expected growth of plants under light.
In science, students compare realistic data with models to test accuracy.

s.defn: Capable of being done or achieved given current resources.
ex: A realistic budget helps ensure project completion.
The plan offers a realistic timeline with built in delays.

s.defn: Broad used to describe something wide in width or extent; not narrow.
ex: The broad river required a longer bridge to span.
A broad coastline provides many study sites for erosion.

s.defn: Broad used to describe general or inclusive in scope, covering many topics or categories; not detailed.
ex: The teacher gave a broad overview of the chapter.
This book offers a broad overview of the topic before the details.

s.defn: The social science that studies how individuals, firms, and governments allocate scarce resources to satisfy wants through production, exchange, and consumption.
ex: Economics explains how households allocate scarce resources.
The field models market behavior and policy outcomes.

s.defn: An academic discipline that develops theories, constructs models, and applies empirical methods to analyze economic phenomena.
ex: In economics, researchers test hypotheses using data.
Graduate programs teach econometrics and microeconomic theory.

s.defn: Applied economics refers to the use of economic theory and empirical methods to analyze real world policy issues and business decisions.
ex: Policy makers rely on applied economics to assess programs.
Businesses study applied economics to optimize resource allocation.

s.defn: The state of being widely known and celebrated in public life, often with positive connotations.
ex: The scientist achieved international fame through the discovery.
Her fame in anthropology grew with the landmark study.

s.defn: The extent of public recognition achieved within a particular domain or field.
ex: Her fame within mathematics grew after the 2012 paper.
The athlete's fame in track and field has drawn sponsorships.

s.defn: The act of planning, organizing, and directing the activities of a group or project.
ex: The school administration approved the new schedule.
Efficient administration helps teachers plan lessons.

s.defn: The act of giving medicines or vaccines to a patient.
ex: Nurse bedside administration of the vaccine occurred today.
Precise administration of medications reduces the risk of errors.

s.defn: The period of time a person or government holds an official position.
ex: The president's administration lasted four years and introduced reforms.
During the administration, the city expanded public services.

s.defn: to provide the means or ability for someone to do something by supplying resources, support, or permission that makes it possible.
ex: The tutoring program will enable students to finish assignments on time.
A scholarship can enable a student to attend a science camp.

s.defn: to turn on or activate a feature or function in a system, device, or software.
ex: Click to enable the calculator tool in the math app.
Admins can enable parental controls to guide student use.

s.defn: A mathematical operation that maps a function or data set to another form, often revealing different representations such as frequency components.
ex: The Fourier transform converts a signal from time to frequency.
A Laplace transform helps solve differential equations in engineering.

s.defn: In geometry, a transform is a rule that moves or changes a figure in position orientation or size while preserving certain properties.
ex: Rotation is a transform that spins a figure around a point.
Translation moves every point the same distance in a chosen direction.

s.defn: to change the form, appearance, or nature of something.
ex: The artist will transform clay into a sculpture.
A caterpillar can transform into a butterfly.

s.defn: to change energy or information from one form to another
ex: Energy can be transformed into electricity.
We transformed the raw data into a chart.

s.defn: to undergo a significant change in form or character
ex: The cocoon will transform into a butterfly.
A good book can transform a reader's thinking.

s.defn: A crop is a plant grown on a farm to be harvested.
ex: Small farms plant corn as their main crop.
This field produced a large crop of wheat.

s.defn: A crop is a batch of items produced at one time.
ex: A crop of new textbooks arrived at the library.
The company released a crop of software updates.

s.defn: To cut or trim the ends or edges of something to make it neat or shorter.
ex: The gardener crops the hedge to keep it neat.
She crops the ends of the hair for a tidy style.

s.defn: To harvest crops from a field or garden.
ex: Farmers crop the field after the rain.
If the fruit is ripe, workers crop the orchard.

s.defn: To appear or occur suddenly or unexpectedly.
ex: Occasional problems crop up during experiments.
Unexpected questions crop up in class discussions.

s.defn: To trim or crop a photograph or image.
ex: The editor crops the image to remove distractions.
Students crop photos to focus on the main subject.

s.defn: Unpleasant or disagreeable in sensory qualities or behavior.
ex: The odor in the room was nasty and hindered the experiment.
Her remarks were nasty and unprofessional in a scholarly setting.

s.defn: Morally offensive or repugnant; ethically unacceptable.
ex: The policy language relied on a nasty stereotype that distorted the analysis.
Cheating is a nasty breach of academic integrity.

s.defn: Very bad or severe in degree or intensity; exceptionally negative in its consequences.
ex: The storm delivered a nasty shock to coastal infrastructure.
Participants faced a nasty risk when the equipment failed.

s.defn: Dirty or grimy; physically dirty or contaminated.
ex: The lab floor was filthy after the spill.
A nasty spill left the bench grimy.

s.defn: An interjection used to express strong disgust or revulsion toward a situation, object, or event; used in informal academic discourse to signal disapproval or discomfort.
ex: Nasty! exclaimed the reviewer upon discovering the contaminated dataset.
Nasty! the auditor hissed, indicating a data integrity breach.

s.defn: An interjection used to condemn or emphasize severity or moral disapproval in response to an ethical breach methodological flaw or unacceptable outcome observed in scholarly work.
ex: Nasty! she exclaimed condemning the protocol violation.
Nasty! the panel concluded critiquing the manipulation of results.

s.defn: The act or process of making information publicly available by printing or posting digitally.
ex: The publication of the science report followed careful review.
Teachers discuss how publication shares ideas with families.

s.defn: A published work such as a book or article that has been made public.
ex: The latest publication in the science journal contains new findings.
Every classroom library carries a varied publication list for readers.

s.defn: A periodical that is issued regularly such as a magazine or newspaper.
ex: Our classroom subscribes to a weekly magazine.
A school library holds several journals and newspapers.

s.defn: An official public announcement or notice issued for information.
ex: The district issued a public publication about schedule changes.
Parents received a notice as a district publication.

s.defn: Confidence in the reliability, truth, or ability of a person, object, or idea.
ex: Experimental research often assumes trust in measurement instruments across trials.
Scholarly discourse treats trust as essential for cooperation among participants.

s.defn: A fiduciary arrangement in which property or assets are held by a trustee for the beneficiaries.
ex: Trust deeds are used to formalize asset management and distribution.
Beneficiaries receive income from a trust instrument according to the instrument's terms.

s.defn: The level of confidence placed by individuals or groups in institutions, processes, or systems.
ex: Public trust in regulatory agencies affects policy effectiveness.
Researchers examine how social trust influences compliance with civic norms.

s.defn: To have confidence in the reliability, truth, or ability of someone or something; to rely on.
ex: Researchers trust the sensor data to reflect real conditions.
Consumers trust brand claims when safety is discussed.

s.defn: To commit something to the care of someone else; to entrust with responsibility or safekeeping.
ex: The charity entrusts volunteers with donated funds.
The board entrusted the project to the senior manager.

s.defn: To place trust in a process or mechanism to function correctly or safely; to rely on its operation.
ex: Manufacturers trust the algorithm to flag anomalies.
Users trust the backup system to recover data.

s.defn: Wealth is money and valuable possessions, the state of having a lot of money and resources.
ex: A family with savings and investments has more wealth than one without.
Wealth can be inherited or earned through work.

s.defn: Wealth is a large amount or abundance of something, such as information or opportunities.
ex: The library offers a wealth of information for students.
A wealth of opportunities awaits learners who study hard.

s.defn: Wealth is the overall material well‑being of a person, family, or nation, indicating economic prosperity.
ex: The nation's wealth grew after new industries formed.
A strong economy increases national wealth over time.

s.defn: In the near past; recently; used to describe events that have occurred not long ago, especially in academic or classroom contexts.
ex: Lately our science lessons have focused on measurement.
Lately students have collected more data to support conclusions.

s.defn: The underground part of a plant that anchors the plant and absorbs water and minerals.
ex: The plant's root absorbs water from the soil.
Researchers map root depth to study drought tolerance.

s.defn: The source or origin of something; the starting point from which development arises.
ex: The root of the theory is based on observation.
Scientists seek the root of the problem to prevent recurrence.

s.defn: The value that, when raised to a specified power, yields a given number; commonly the square root.
ex: The square root of nine equals three.
Find the cube root of twenty seven.

s.defn: In linguistics, the base morpheme or stem of a word that carries core meaning, to which affixes attach.
ex: In many languages the root carries core meaning.
The word happiness has the root happy as its base.

s.defn: To cause a plant cutting to form roots so that it can grow as a new plant.
ex: Gardeners root cuttings in damp soil to propagate new plants.
Stems will root in water and form a new plant.

s.defn: To be the basis or origin of something; to be firmly established or derived from.
ex: The tradition roots its values in ancient beliefs.
The theory roots in data from several studies.

s.defn: A noun meaning the act of jumping or dropping into water, usually headfirst, for sport or recreation.
ex: The swimmer practiced a clean headfirst dive.
In class, we learned to enter water with a front dive.

s.defn: A dirty or disreputable bar or tavern, especially one that is inexpensive.
ex: We avoided that dive on Main Street.
The dive offered cheap drinks and music.

s.defn: An in-depth examination or exploration of a topic or issue.
ex: The class did a deep dive into the water cycle.
The science teacher invited a deep dive on ecosystems.

s.defn: To plunge headfirst into water, typically from a surface or platform.
ex: The swimmer practiced a safe headfirst dive from the springboard.
Lifeguards monitor students to ensure the dive is controlled.

s.defn: To start doing something with energy and focus, or to study something deeply.
ex: Students dive into the lab activity with curiosity.
Readers dive into a challenging topic with focus.

s.defn: To submerge or descend beneath the surface of water.
ex: Divers dive to observe life on the ocean floor.
The submarine dived deeper after the signal.

s.defn: To fall quickly or drop sharply, as numbers or prices.
ex: Stock prices dived after the report.
Temperatures dived to record lows during the night.

s.defn: A random is an outcome or event produced by chance, not predetermined.
ex: The roll of a die yields a random outcome.
In experiments, random outcomes can vary from trial to trial.

s.defn: Not planned or organized; lacking a definite pattern or purpose.
ex: The seating is arranged in a random order to avoid bias.
The teacher used a random layout for questions to minimize predictability.

s.defn: Describing a process or selection made by chance rather than by a fixed rule.
ex: In the classroom, students were assigned to groups by randomization to prevent bias.
A random sample of students was drawn for the survey.

s.defn: To cause something to be certain to occur or be the case by taking necessary actions.
ex: In experimental design, randomization is used to ensure internal validity.
Researchers must ensure participants meet eligibility criteria.

s.defn: To guarantee the availability or occurrence of something through planned action or provision of resources, often to secure funding, resources, or compliance with standards.
ex: The grant terms require periodic reporting to ensure ongoing funding.
Quality management procedures ensure regulatory compliance across suppliers.

s.defn: In computing and information management, to maintain data integrity, invariants, or system states by checks, validations, or monitoring.
ex: The database enforces constraints to ensure data integrity.
During replication, checkpoints are used to ensure consistency across nodes.

s.defn: Relating to the countryside or nonurban areas; characterized by open spaces, farms, and dispersed settlement.
ex: The rural landscape features farmland and hedgerows, offering field biology opportunities.
Rural communities often rely on local markets and cooperative farming.

s.defn: Describing programs, policies, or life patterns associated with agriculture and countryside, especially in contrast to urban settings.
ex: Rural development programs focus on roads and schools in remote districts.
Health surveys compare rural and urban populations to identify disparities.

s.defn: A small amount of salty liquid secreted by the eye, especially in response to emotion or irritation.

Students documented teardrops forming as the character faced hardship.

s.defn: A rip or opening in something caused by tearing.
ex: A tear in the fabric allowed cold air to enter the classroom.
The paper displayed a large tear near the margin after handling.

s.defn: To pull something apart or into pieces by force.
ex: The strong wind tore the flag from its post.
She tore the page in half during class.

s.defn: To move rapidly or travel quickly.
ex: The car tore down the road in seconds.
Time tore by while we waited.

s.defn: To cause someone to cry or be moved to tears.
ex: The sad news tore him up.
Seeing the old photo tears me up.

s.defn: To keep possession of something and not lose it over time.
ex: The school will retain student records for five years.
Students should retain key notes after the lesson.

s.defn: To remember or store information in one’s memory.
ex: Regular study helps students retain vocabulary.
Mnemonic devices help you retain facts.

s.defn: To hire or engage a professional or service.
ex: We retained a lawyer to review the contract.
The homeschooling family retained a math tutor.

s.defn: The monetary charge assessed for travel on public transport or for a service; the price demanded for passage or service.
ex: The subway fare increased by 5 percent after the fare review.
Elasticity of demand with respect to fare changes was the subject of the study.

s.defn: The food served or prepared as part of a meal; the kind of dishes offered by an establishment.
ex: The market offers a diverse fare of European dishes.
This restaurant specializes in Italian fare.

s.defn: To manage or progress in a given situation; to experience a specified outcome, typically described as doing well or poorly.
ex: The students fared well after the tutoring program.
Small firms fared poorly during the recession.

s.defn: To travel or proceed in a specified direction or manner, especially in a historical or literary sense.
ex: The expedition fared northward through the pass.
The vessel fared westward during the gale.

s.defn: Help such as food medicine or shelter given to people after disasters wars or shortages.
ex: The classroom studied how humanitarian relief reached refugees after the flood.
Local volunteers organized a disaster aid convoy to deliver blankets and food.

s.defn: A sculpted image carved so figures project from or sit within a flat background used in monuments and art.

The teacher explained how bas relief shows figures raised from a flat surface.

s.defn: A military action that frees a town or fortress by bringing supplies or troops to end a siege or danger.
ex: In history class students read how a relief force lifted the siege of the city.
The commander led a reinforcement to protect the town from enemy capture.

s.defn: Religious: sacred or consecrated; set apart for reverence and worship; objects, places, days, or persons venerated within a tradition.
ex: Ancient relics within the temple are treated as holy.
The holy day is observed with fasting and prayer.

s.defn: Informal intensifier: used as a modifier to convey extreme degree or emphasis when describing a noun or adjective, particularly in colloquial speech.
ex: That proposal turned out to be a holy mess.
The team faced a holy challenge to meet the deadline.

s.defn: The sacred status or state of being holy, recognized within a religious or moral context as worthy of reverence.
ex: The sacred status of relics shapes ritual practice across traditions.
Sanctity anchors ethical norms in many societies.

s.defn: A person or object regarded as holy within a religious tradition; a sacred person or thing.
ex: Pilgrims approach the relic with reverence and careful ritual.
The saint's image became a focal point of worship.

s.defn: The act of showing how something works or why it is true to help learning.
ex: The science teacher did a demonstration to show how photosynthesis works.
A quick demonstration helps students see the rule in math.

s.defn: A public gathering intended to express support or opposition to an issue.
ex: People joined a peaceful protest near the city hall.
The demonstration drew reporters and a large crowd.

s.defn: A formal proof or clear example used to establish a fact in math or science.
ex: A geometric demonstration shows why triangles are similar.
The algebraic demonstration explains how to solve for x.

s.defn: Characterized by a persistent mood of sadness or low affect; lacking enthusiasm or interest; observed in affective states.
ex: A depressed mood is common in patients with major depressive disorder.
Researchers assess depressed mood using standardized affect scales.

s.defn: In economics, a depressed economy is characterized by prolonged low growth or contraction, high unemployment, and weak demand.
ex: Several regions entered a depressed economy after factory closures.
Policy measures aimed to revive demand in a depressed economy.

s.defn: Having an indentation or sunken region relative to surrounding areas; produced by compression or impact; a depressed surface feature.
ex: The alloy showed a depressed region on the surface after processing.
Metallurgical analysis identified a depressed region due to uneven cooling.

s.defn: To cause a person to feel sad, discouraged, or despondent.
ex: The unexpected dismissal depressed the team's morale.

s.defn: In economics, to reduce price levels or economic activity, leading to lower demand or profits.
ex: Policy measures depressed investment and hiring.
Weak consumer demand depressed quarterly earnings.

s.defn: To apply downward pressure on a control such as a lever or button.
ex: Depress the brake pedal before shifting.

s.defn: The absence of light in a space.

s.defn: A lack of knowledge or clear understanding.

s.defn: A mood or atmosphere of fear or gloom produced by darkness.
ex: The old house felt ominous in the darkness and cold air.
In literature, darkness often signals danger or moral uncertainty.

s.defn: The property of a group or system that contains a broad range of distinct elements or categories, reflecting heterogeneity and a wide scope of variation.
ex: The classroom exhibits diversity in students' linguistic backgrounds.
Policy aims to increase diversity of thought in research teams.

s.defn: Genetic diversity is the total variation of genetic characteristics within a population, contributing to adaptive potential and resilience.
ex: Populations with greater genetic diversity recover faster after stress.
Conservation efforts aim to maintain genetic diversity in endangered species.

s.defn: The presence of multiple distinct social or cultural groups within a community, institution, or society, including differences in race, ethnicity, language, gender, and perspectives.
ex: Workplaces with diversity of background show greater creativity.
Curricular reforms seek to enhance diversity of perspectives.

s.defn: A plan for spending money during a period showing expected income and expenditures.

The science fair needs a budget for materials.

s.defn: The amount of money allocated for a specific purpose or project; the funded sum set aside.

The event budget sets aside money for decorations and snacks.

s.defn: To plan and control the amount of money to be spent on a project or activity by creating a budget.
ex: The teacher budgets classroom supplies for the month.

s.defn: To estimate the cost of a project or item and assign a planned amount for spending.
ex: The budget estimates the cost of the science project.
They budget the field trip before permissions are asked.

s.defn: To allocate time or other resources for a task by setting aside a specific amount of time.
ex: We budget time for reading and writing.
Students learn to budget time for experiments.

s.defn: Inexpensive; affordable or low in price, suitable for classroom use when funds are limited.
ex: The science kit was budget-friendly and fits our classroom limit.
We chose the affordable lab mats to stay within our budget.

s.defn: Relating to a plan of spending prepared in advance for school purchases.
ex: The budgeted amount for science supplies is limited.
We kept a budgeted plan for field trip expenses.

s.defn: The extent or area that something covers or reaches; the distance or area over which something is distributed.

The spread of light across the classroom wall.

s.defn: A meal or assortment of foods served together; a large number of dishes prepared for eating.

s.defn: The act or process of spreading or dissemination; the extent to which something has spread.

s.defn: To lay out or distribute over a surface so as to cover a larger area.

s.defn: To extend over a wide area or distance; to reach into more space or people.

News of the event spread across the campus.

s.defn: To cause information, ideas, or illnesses to be transmitted widely among people; to become known by many.
ex: Gossip spread through the class.
A rumor spread quickly after lunch.

s.defn: To be against or resist a proposal, policy, or idea.

s.defn: To be in competition with someone or something; to face off against an opponent in a game or contest.

s.defn: To present an opposing argument or counteract a claim with evidence.

s.defn: The fleshy portion of the face that forms the lateral aspect below the eye, comprising subcutaneous fat and muscles.
ex: Anatomical measurements were taken at the cheek region.
Swelling of the cheek occurred after the injury.

s.defn: Audacious insolence or impudence in speech or behavior.
ex: The student showed cheek when questioned about the results.

s.defn: To address or speak to someone with impudent boldness or insolent backtalk; to challenge or show disrespect through verbal interaction.
ex: The student cheeked the supervisor by interrupting to challenge the assessment criteria.

s.defn: The visible, gaseous portion of a fire produced by the heating and oxidation of a combustible material, typically emitting light and heat.

s.defn: A hostile or insulting message posted in an online discussion, typically intended to provoke or belittle another user.
ex: The commenter posted a flame in the thread.

s.defn: A strong emotion of intense liking or passion; ardor or enthusiasm directed toward a person, idea, or activity.

s.defn: A flame used as a heat source in laboratory or industrial equipment, typically a gas or oil flame produced by a burner.

s.defn: To ignite or cause to burn with flame; to set alight by applying heat or a flame.
ex: The substrate was flame treated to remove surface oxides.

s.defn: In schooling, an examination is a formal assessment designed to measure a student's knowledge or skills in a subject, typically for a grade or score.

Teachers use classroom examinations to check understanding.

s.defn: An examination is the careful inspection or analysis of something to gather information, verify facts, or judge quality.
ex: The scientist performed an examination of the sample under a microscope.
A careful examination of the text revealed key themes.

s.defn: A fixed or prolonged look directed at a person or object, typically sustained without movement.
ex: The subject's fixed stare persisted during the visual task.

s.defn: An act of looking steadily at someone or something, often signaling assessment, interest, or social surveillance.

The courtroom footage highlighted the witness's stare as an index of credibility assessment.

s.defn: To look at something with fixed eyes for an extended period, typically in response to concentration, surprise, or interest.

s.defn: To fix one's gaze on a person or object in a manner intended to intimidate or impose dominance, often by maintaining prolonged eye contact.

s.defn: To look at something with a fixed and unfocused gaze, often during daydreaming, reverie, or cognitive disengagement.

s.defn: A noun denoting the tactile sensation or texture of a surface; the perceived quality produced by touch.

s.defn: A noun indicating the general impression or atmosphere of a place, situation, or work.

s.defn: A noun denoting an emotional state or subjective sensation experienced by a person; an affective feeling.

s.defn: A noun denoting an intuitive ability or natural aptitude for a field or activity; a feel for something.

s.defn: Perceive via tactile contact or physical surface sensation; to come into contact with a material or object and register a tactile or somatosensory experience.

s.defn: Experience an emotional or affective state or impression; to undergo an internal cognitive or affective experience.

s.defn: A physiological sensation of discomfort or weakness caused by the need for food.

s.defn: A strong nonliteral desire or craving for something not related to food, such as knowledge or power.

s.defn: To have a strong desire or craving for something; to long for or want strongly.

s.defn: The faculty of sight; the sense by which living beings perceive light, color, and form.

s.defn: The ability to imagine future possibilities and plan ahead.

s.defn: A mental image seen during sleep or a vivid dream.

s.defn: An aspirational description of what an organization or group aims to achieve.

s.defn: A prime number is a natural number greater than 1 that has no positive divisors other than 1 and itself.

s.defn: The prime of life is the period during which a person is at peak physical and mental condition.

s.defn: To prepare or make ready (someone or something) for a specified purpose or upcoming action by providing resources, instructions, or conditions.
ex: Researchers prime the study by standardizing protocols and materials.
The instructor primes participants with the necessary briefing before experiments.

s.defn: To apply primer to a surface to enhance adhesion of subsequent coatings.
ex: The technician primed the wall before applying topcoat.
Apply primer and then prime the surface.

s.defn: To influence or bias someone’s expectations or responses by introducing particular cues or information beforehand.
ex: The experiment primed subjects with neutral cues before the task.
Researchers primed participants' expectations by describing potential outcomes.

s.defn: Of primary importance; forming the most important or central aspect in a given context.
ex: The prime objective of the study is to minimize error.
A prime location often determines the feasibility of fieldwork.

s.defn: Of the highest quality or value; top-grade or prime in condition.
ex: Prime beef is valued for tenderness and flavor.
We selected a prime supplier offering high grade materials.

s.defn: The area, environment, and objects surrounding a place or thing.
ex: The surrounding area was heavily forested.
Researchers mapped the surrounding environment to study habitat edges.

s.defn: The act of encircling or enclosing; the boundary or enclosure formed around something.
ex: The surrounding of the field by a fence was completed.
Encirclement constitutes the surrounding of the site by security barriers.

s.defn: To form a boundary around an object or area by enclosing it on all sides; to encircle.
ex: The fortress is surrounded by a defensive wall.
A hedge surrounds the garden to delineate the boundary.

s.defn: Situated on or around the outer edge; encircling.
ex: The surrounding ring of trees provides habitat for wildlife.
Surrounding soil conditions influenced plant growth in the experiment.

s.defn: Located in the area near a reference point; in the vicinity.
ex: Nearby sampling sites were selected to capture variance in surrounding conditions.
Surrounding neighborhoods were surveyed for demographic variability.

s.defn: Relating to the context or external factors surrounding a subject; contextual.
ex: The surrounding context was considered in interpreting the results.
Surrounding factors confounded the observed association.

s.defn: A bound collection of items tied or gathered together; a cluster or bundle.
ex: a bunch of grapes hung from the vine
the gardener gathered a bunch of flowers from the bed

s.defn: A crowd or informal grouping of people assembled in one place.
ex: a large bunch of students gathered after the lecture
the committee was a tight bunch at the meeting

s.defn: A large quantity or number of items, often used informally.
ex: the study produced a bunch of data points for analysis
they offered a bunch of discount offers during the sale

s.defn: to form into a cluster or group; to gather into a compact mass.
ex: The data points were bunched into clusters for analysis.
Researchers bunched the samples to reduce variance.

s.defn: to press or crowd into a tighter formation, usually by applying pressure; to become crowded or compacted.
ex: The fabric tended to bunch when stretched, reducing permeability.
Excess material will cause the seam to bunch, impairing fit.

s.defn: Done by choice and not required.
ex: Participation is voluntary in the science lab.
Students may choose an optional reading task.

s.defn: Relating to volunteering or to acts performed by volunteers without pay.
ex: The voluntary program relies on student volunteers.
Many clubs promote voluntary service projects.

s.defn: To a complete extent; without qualification, modifying a verb, adjective, or other adverb to indicate total degree or scope.
ex: The results were entirely consistent with the hypothesis.
The protocol is entirely automated and requires no manual input.

s.defn: A person who actively pursues something desired, such as information, knowledge, or achievement.
ex: A seeker of knowledge attends lectures and reads extensively.
Job seekers use employment portals to find opportunities.

s.defn: A person who searches for information, data, or sources as part of research or learning.
ex: Information seekers consult libraries and databases to locate sources.
Researchers act as information seekers during systematic reviews.

s.defn: A person who pursues spiritual or philosophical truth, often within religious or contemplative contexts.
ex: Spiritual seekers explore meditation and contemplation.
Truth seekers challenge conventional beliefs in scholarly discourse.

s.defn: To place or deliver something for evaluation, approval, or decision by another person or authority.
ex: Students submit assignments by the due date.
Researchers submit manuscripts to journals for publication.

s.defn: To yield to or accept the authority or control of another person or body.
ex: The students submitted to the classroom rules without question.
The citizens submitted to the new safety regulations after the vote.

s.defn: To present for consideration or review by others, typically a plan or document in a formal setting.
ex: Teachers submit proposals for class projects.
Researchers submit grant applications for funding.

s.defn: A particular way of thinking about something; a point of view.
ex: From a scientific perspective this method yields reliable results.
Her perspective on the issue changed after reading new data.

s.defn: In art and geometry, the technique of representing depth on a flat surface.
ex: Artists use perspective to show depth on a flat canvas.
In geometry class we study one point perspective.

s.defn: A personal or group outlook shaped by experiences; a frame of reference used to interpret situations.
ex: From a historical perspective the event shaped policy.
From an economic perspective the study highlights costs.

s.defn: A thing that must be done or provided as part of a task or program.
ex: Completing the reading log is a requirement for the science project.
Bringing a signed permission slip is a requirement for the field trip.

s.defn: A condition that must be met to qualify for something or to finish a step in an activity.
ex: A minimum test score is a requirement for admission to the program.
Letters of recommendation are a requirement for the upper grade level.

s.defn: A formal obligation imposed by law, policy, or contract.
ex: A safety inspection is a legal requirement for factories.
Tax forms include a parental consent requirement.

s.defn: Of or relating to the color or appearance of gold; having a bright, metallic yellow hue.
ex: The metal displayed a golden hue under standard illumination.
Gold nanoparticles exhibit a golden color due to surface plasmon resonance.

s.defn: Of or relating to a material consisting of gold or finished with a gold coating; having the properties of gold in composition or surface.
ex: The ring is made of gold.
The coin shows a golden finish.

s.defn: Having the quality of being extremely favorable or advantageous; particularly suitable or valuable.
ex: The proposal represented a golden opportunity for expansion.
The grant provided a golden opportunity for collaboration.

s.defn: Used to describe an ideal or highly desirable period, standard, or state; often appearing in fixed expressions.
ex: The Renaissance is often described as a golden age.
The company aimed to set a gold standard for safety.

s.defn: An adverb indicating any location at which an action occurs; used to refer to any place where something happens, without specifying a particular location.
ex: Wherever the data were collected, the protocol was followed.
Wherever the samples are located, measurements were recorded consistently.

s.defn: A disjunctive adverb used to generalize a statement across locations, often introducing a dependent clause and signaling that the assertion applies regardless of where it occurs.
ex: Wherever possible, researchers should provide full citations.
Wherever the study takes place, ethical guidelines apply.

s.defn: A subordinating conjunction that introduces a clause describing any location or circumstance in which a statement holds, equivalent to no matter where.
ex: Wherever data are missing, imputation methods were applied.
Wherever feasible, randomized sampling was employed to reduce bias.

s.defn: Protected from danger or harm; not likely to be harmed.
ex: The secure data was encrypted to prevent access.
Students should keep personal information in a secure location.

s.defn: Fixed firmly in place; not loose or liable to move.
ex: The secure lid prevents accidental spills.
The panel is secured with four bolts.

s.defn: Free from doubt; reliable or guaranteed; providing trust or certainty.
ex: The secure protocol ensures data integrity.
Researchers require secure methods to confirm conclusions.

s.defn: To fasten or fix something in place so that it cannot move.
ex: The science kit was secured to the workbench with clamps.
The cables were secured along the bench to prevent accidents.

s.defn: To obtain or guarantee something through effort, such as funding or access.
ex: The group worked to secure funding for the science project.
The project team secured a grant after presenting their proposal.

s.defn: To protect someone or something from danger or loss; to keep safe or private.
ex: The school secures student records by encryption.
Teachers secure online accounts with password protection.

s.defn: A league is a group of teams or clubs that compete against each other.
ex: Several schools formed a league to compete in soccer.
Teams in the league schedule interscholastic matches each season.

s.defn: A league is a historical unit of distance equal to about three miles.
ex: Historically a league measured about three miles.
Ancient maps show distances in leagues rather than kilometers.

s.defn: To form or join a league with others; to ally for a shared purpose.
ex: Countries leagued with neighboring states to counter the threat.
Schools leaguing to share resources and expertise.

s.defn: A fixed payment charged in exchange for goods or a service.
ex: The library charges an admission fee for workshops.
Students pay a service fee when using school printers.

s.defn: A payment required by an authority to obtain permission, certification, or access.
ex: A licensing fee is required to operate a small business.
The renewal fee is due each year for vehicle registrations.

s.defn: Of or relating to events or conditions causing extreme distress or misfortune; lamentable or disastrous in consequence.
ex: The collapse of the program had tragic consequences for patients and communities.
A tragic miscalculation by the planners led to widespread losses.

s.defn: Relating to tragedy or to the literary genre of tragedy; characterized by a serious, somber, or fatal tone in drama or narrative.
ex: Scholars analyze tragic drama to understand the portrayal of hamartia.
The term is used to describe a tragic ending in classical tragedy.

s.defn: An icon is a symbol or image used to represent a concept, object, or action.
ex: In art history, a dove can serve as an icon for peace.
Textbooks describe icons as simple pictures that stand for ideas.

s.defn: A famous person who is widely admired as a representative example or model.
ex: A cultural icon such as Gandhi is studied in history to illustrate leadership.
Biographies describe icons of innovation who inspire students to pursue science.

s.defn: A sacred religious painting or image used in worship, especially in Orthodox Christian traditions.
ex: Students study medieval icons to understand religious symbolism and technique.
Orthodox studies analyze an icon's materials and method of creation.

s.defn: In computing, a small graphical symbol on a computer interface that represents a program, file, or action.
ex: Students learn to identify app icons on the tablet home screen.
In computing, icons help users locate programs quickly.

s.defn: To be unlike or not the same as another thing.
ex: The two ecosystems differ in rainfall patterns.
Leaf shapes differ between the species.

s.defn: To hold or express a different opinion from someone else.
ex: Students differ with the textbook's conclusion.
Researchers may differ from earlier studies due to new data.

s.defn: In mathematics or measurement, to have a value that is not equal to another; to yield a different result when compared.
ex: The results differ by 0.5 units between methods.
Measured values differ across trials.

s.defn: In general academic usage, the adjective cute denotes something aesthetically pleasing and endearing, typically small or youthful in appearance, prompting affectionate appraisal.
ex: The infants were rated as cute by observers in the experiment.
The dataset notes a correlation between cuteness and rapid approach responses.

s.defn: In scholarly contexts, cute also refers to a solution, design, or idea that is clever, elegant, or ingeniously simple, often characterized by economy of means.
ex: The algorithm is a cute solution to the subproblem, though not scalable.
A cute workaround reduces time complexity in the pilot study.

s.defn: In informal or nontechnical discourse, cute is used to convey positive appraisal or friendliness, often softening critique or indicating approval in social science and humanities contexts.
ex: The author notes the term cute can ease reader engagement in qualitative studies.
Using cute as a descriptor may bias interpretation in field surveys.

s.defn: Expression used as an interjection to express positive appraisal of a subject's charm or appeal.
ex: During the pilot study a participant exclaimed Cute at the novel stimulus.
The coder noted a Cute response to the interface prototype.

s.defn: Ironical interjection signaling mild skepticism or mocking approval of an attempt or claim.
ex: The reviewer offered Cute, signaling mild irony about the method.
The transcript shows Cute as a sarcastic confirmation of the claim.

s.defn: A person who has authority or control over others or over a place or thing; the person in charge.
ex: The ship's master issued orders.
The project master supervised the team during the experiment.

s.defn: A person who has attained high level skill or mastery in a craft or field; an expert.
ex: He is a master carpenter.
She is a master of ceremonies.

s.defn: The original version or primary copy from which duplicates are produced.
ex: The master copy was archived after editing.
The master recording is kept in secure storage.

s.defn: Academic degree awarded after completion of graduate study; the masters degree.
ex: She earned a master's degree.
The program offers a Master of Science.

s.defn: To acquire complete knowledge or skill in a subject or technique through study and practice, resulting in a high level of proficiency.
ex: She mastered the piano after years of practice.
Students must master calculus to complete the physics program.

s.defn: To gain control of a situation or device; to manage or command with skill and confidence.
ex: He mastered the situation by staying calm.
The pilot mastered the landing sequence despite weather.

s.defn: To produce a master copy for distribution from which duplicates are made; to complete the mastering process of a recording, document, or data set.
ex: The engineer mastered the track for release.
We mastered the documentary to optimize sound levels.

s.defn: Of or relating to exceptional skill or mastery; indicating expert proficiency.
ex: The master carpenter completed the joint with flawless precision.
A master printer demonstrated flawless alignment during the press run.

s.defn: Designating the main or primary item; of chief importance or authority.
ex: The master plan guided the redevelopment project.
The master switch controls power to the entire system.

s.defn: A sheet or band of flexible material used to cover, enclose, or protect an object, typically a thin film such as plastic, foil, or paper.
ex: The plastic wrap kept the fruit fresh.
Use a protective wrap to seal the parcel.

s.defn: A garment consisting of a length of fabric draped around the body, typically worn over the shoulders or upper body.
ex: She draped a silk wrap over her shoulders.
At the ceremony, he wore a lightweight wrap.

s.defn: A food item consisting of a folded or rolled flatbread such as a tortilla enclosing fillings.
ex: The lunch menu includes a chicken wrap.
She ordered a veggie wrap with avocado.

s.defn: To enclose or cover an object by winding or folding a material around it, typically for protection, concealment, or presentation.
ex: The researcher wrapped the specimen in aluminum foil to prevent contamination.
The package was wrapped in protective paper prior to shipment.

s.defn: To conclude or finish a discussion, report, or event; to bring something to a close.
ex: The committee wrapped up the session with a summary of findings.
The editor wrapped up the article with a brief discussion of limitations.

s.defn: Wraparound describes an adjective use denoting surrounding or enclosing on all sides, forming a continuous boundary around a central element.
ex: The wraparound boundary minimizes edge effects in the simulation.
A wraparound porch extends interior spaces to the outdoors.

s.defn: Wrappable describes something that can be wrapped or covered with a wrapping.
ex: The fabric is wrappable and suitable for rapid repairs.
The material is wrapable and suitable for wrapping.

s.defn: Wrap clothing refers to garments designed to be tied or wrapped around the body, typically featuring an adjustable fit.
ex: In the study, wrap clothing facilitates adjustable mobility during tasks.
Ethnographic accounts describe wrap garments as culturally significant forms of attire.

s.defn: A form of government in which power is held by the people, either directly or through elected representatives.
ex: Constitutional democracy guarantees rights while enabling citizen elections.
In many democracies, elections empower citizens to choose leaders.

s.defn: The doctrine or principle that power should be held by the people, promoting political equality and civil liberties.
ex: Scholars compare democracy with various political ideologies in class discussions.
Textbooks describe democracy as both an ideal and a practical system.

s.defn: A belief that someone or something will be reliable and worthy of trust.
ex: The student answered with confidence about the science project.
We have confidence in the teacher's instructions.

s.defn: The belief in one's own abilities and worth.
ex: She spoke with poise during the presentation.
Daily practice boosts her competence and confidence.

s.defn: The degree of certainty that a result or plan will occur or be true.
ex: The forecast gives high confidence that rain will arrive tomorrow.
Her data increased confidence that the hypothesis was true.

s.defn: A secret told to a trusted person; private information.
ex: She told a confidence to her friend.
Keeping confidences protects privacy and trust.

s.defn: A physiological or psychological dependence on a substance that motivates continued use and withdrawal avoidance.
ex: Physiological dependence on alcohol often accompanies withdrawal symptoms.
Withdrawal symptoms complicate the treatment of drug addiction.

s.defn: A habitual behavioral pattern that involves compulsive engagement in rewarding activities, leading to impairment or distress, without a primary chemical substance.
ex: Behavioral addictions may occur without chemical involvement.
Shopping addiction can co-occur with mood disorders.

s.defn: A medical or psychiatric disorder characterized by compulsive engagement in rewarding stimuli despite adverse consequences, often requiring integrated treatment.
ex: Substance use disorder is diagnosed when impairment due to use persists.
Gambling disorder has been classified as a behavioral addiction in clinical manuals.

s.defn: A device made of parts that work together to produce a motion or result.
ex: The mechanism inside a bicycle brake converts rider force into stopping power.
A simple lever mechanism multiplies effort to lift a load.

s.defn: The set of causes or steps that explain how something happens.
ex: Scientists study the mechanism of digestion to explain how nutrients are absorbed.
Teachers discuss the mechanism behind photosynthesis to help students understand it.

s.defn: A formal plan or method used to achieve a goal.
ex: A school uses a reward mechanism to encourage good behavior.
The classroom uses a praise mechanism to reinforce routines.

s.defn: A structured set of questions used to collect information from respondents in research, typically administered in surveys to measure variables.
ex: Researchers distributed a questionnaire to participants to assess attitudes toward policy.
A 30-item questionnaire gauged knowledge and attitudes about the topic.

s.defn: The document or digital file that contains the questions, including administration instructions, response options, and coding rules.
ex: The online questionnaire form included skip patterns.
Researchers stored the paper questionnaire form as backup.

s.defn: To administer a questionnaire to respondents as part of a research study in order to collect structured data.
ex: The researchers questionnaireed 350 students to assess study habits.
The team questionnaireed participants online to gather demographic information.

s.defn: lasting for a long time or forever; not temporary.
ex: A permanent record is kept for student grades.
A permanent solution requires long term planning.

s.defn: fixed and unchanging; not easily altered.
ex: The policy should be permanent once adopted.
A permanent fixture stays in place year after year.

s.defn: A long passage inside a building that connects rooms or areas, enabling movement between them.
ex: Researchers walked along the hospital corridor to reach patient rooms.
A quiet corridor connected the museum galleries and study rooms.

s.defn: A channel or pathway through which influence, authority, or information flows within an organization or political system, often used metaphorically.
ex: Scholars describe the corridor of power as a central axis of governance.
In organizational theory, the corridor metaphor denotes informal pathways used to influence decisions.

s.defn: The act or process of making something, especially in industry or production.
ex: The manufacture of bicycles requires careful assembly lines.
The process of manufacture is studied in the lesson.

s.defn: The goods or products that are made by manufacturing; items that have been manufactured.
ex: Manufactured goods must pass inspection before export.
The market studies compare manufactured goods with raw materials.

s.defn: A factory or plant where goods are produced.
ex: The town hosts a textile manufacture that produces fabrics.
A new car manufacture facility opens next year.

s.defn: To manufacture is to make goods or items in large quantities, typically in a factory setting, using machinery.
ex: Factories manufacture consumer electronics using automated assembly lines.
Mass production lowers costs by standardizing processes.

s.defn: To invent or fabricate something, especially information or data, often to mislead.
ex: Some studies were criticized for fabricated results.
Ethics discussions explore how researchers may fabricate data.

s.defn: To plan and assemble parts into a finished whole, often in a design or engineering context.
ex: Students learn to assemble a model kit from instructions.
Design teams assemble components to create prototypes.

s.defn: A sum of money placed into a bank account for safekeeping or credit.
ex: A small deposit was made to the savings account.
Regular deposits help grow the balance over time.

s.defn: A natural accumulation of minerals or other materials in the earth.
ex: Geologists found a gold deposit beneath the hillside.
Alluvial deposits form where rivers slow down.

s.defn: A layer of material that has settled on a surface over time.
ex: A dust deposit covered the classroom shelves.
Rust deposits appeared on the fence after rain.

s.defn: To put money into a bank account or other financial place to save it.
ex: I will deposit five dollars into my savings account today.
She asked the teller to deposit her paycheck into her account this week.

s.defn: To place something somewhere for safekeeping.
ex: Please deposit the books in the box for safekeeping.
We will deposit the letter in the mailbox for safekeeping.

s.defn: To lay down layers of material such as sediment or minerals over time.
ex: Over centuries the lake bed deposits layers of sediment.
Rocks can deposit minerals as veins in the stone.

s.defn: Not honest or truthful; lacking integrity; prone to lying or deception.
ex: The researcher engaged in dishonest data manipulation.
A dishonest study design undermines credibility of results.

s.defn: Characterized by deception or misrepresentation in practice; describing statements, data, or actions intended to mislead.
ex: The journalist published dishonest statistics to sway readers.
The vendor's dishonest advertising violated consumer protection laws.

s.defn: In noun usage, a person who is dishonest; an individual who engages in deceit or fraud.
ex: The dishonest was identified by the committee amid allegations of falsified records.
The dishonest contributed to the scandal by misreporting financial data.

s.defn: The state of being lively and energetic; the quality of liveliness in a person, scene, or performance.
ex: The crowd's animation increased during the demonstration.
Liveliness and animation contribute to engagement in seminars.

s.defn: The process of creating moving images by sequencing discrete drawings or frames, a core technique in cinema and multimedia.
ex: 2D animation is commonly used for traditional cartoons.
Historically cel animation relied on hand drawn frames.

s.defn: In digital graphics, the movement of visual elements to convey change, feedback, or emphasis in user interfaces and data visualizations.
ex: UI designers use animation to indicate state changes and responses.
Data dashboards employ animation to reveal trends during transitions.

s.defn: To discover or come upon something by searching or exploring; to locate something that was hidden or unknown.
ex: Archaeologists found ancient pottery during the dig.
Students found the solution after reviewing the clues.

s.defn: To establish or create something such as an institution, organization, or program.
ex: The university founded a new research center.
A charity was founded to help refugees.

s.defn: Describing something that has been discovered or located.
ex: The found artifacts were cataloged in the lab.
Researchers checked the found documents for dating.

s.defn: An adverb indicating that something happens once every year, typically used when describing schedules, budgets, or annual events.
ex: The science fair is held annually to review yearlong progress.
Students submit progress portfolios annually at the end of the term.

s.defn: The professional activity and occupation of providing patient care by nurses, including assessment, planning, implementation, and evaluation within clinical settings.
ex: The nursing profession requires licensure and ongoing professional development.
Nursing practice increasingly emphasizes interprofessional collaboration and evidence based care.

s.defn: The act of feeding an infant by a lactating caregiver, most commonly through breastfeeding.
ex: Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first six months by major health authorities.
Early initiation of breastfeeding supports maternal infant bonding and lactation.

s.defn: An academic discipline concerned with nursing as a science and profession, encompassing theory development, research, education, and policy.
ex: Nursing theory informs clinical practice and education.
Nursing education programs integrate theory with clinical simulation.

s.defn: To provide medical or caregiving services to a patient, typically as a nurse, by performing tasks such as monitoring, administering medications, and coordinating care.
ex: The staff nurse is nursing the patient in the ward.
Clinical rounds emphasize nursing assessment as central to care planning.

s.defn: To feed or sustain an infant or young animal by nursing, typically by a mother or caregiver.
ex: The mother is nursing her newborn at the breast.
Caregivers must monitor the infant during nursing sessions.

s.defn: To harbor or nurture a feeling, thought, or intention over time, such as a grievance or resentment.
ex: He has been nursing a grievance for years.
She nursed doubts about the project's viability during the review.

s.defn: Relating to the profession or practice of nursing, including patient care activities carried out by registered or licensed nurses.
ex: Nursing practice guidelines were updated in the hospital.
Nursing research informs evidence based patient care.

s.defn: Describing care, interventions, or services delivered by nurses in clinical practice.
ex: Nursing interventions reduced infection rates.
Nursing assessments were performed before surgery.

s.defn: Relating to the education, training, or professional formation of nurses.
ex: Nursing education standards emphasize clinical competencies.
Nursing training programs incorporate simulation and ethics.

s.defn: A person who collects objects, usually as a hobby or for study.
ex: She is a stamp collector who loves studying postal history.
The class visited a local exhibit where a coin collector explained grading coins.

s.defn: An object or device that gathers substances such as dust or rain for measurement or storage.
ex: Factories use a dust collector to keep air clean.
A rain collector stores rainwater for irrigation experiments.

s.defn: The result or effect of an action, plan, or event.
ex: The outcome of the science experiment showed a color change.
Her final project grade was the outcome of the student assessment and homework.

s.defn: One possible result of a random experiment such as a dice roll or coin flip; the collection of all such results forms the sample space.
ex: Roll a die and note the outcome.
The outcome of rolling two dice can range from 2 to 12.

s.defn: In a literal sense, indicating that the words describe reality exactly, without metaphor.
ex: The label literally states the contents are hazardous.
The manual literally lists the safety steps in order.

s.defn: Used as an informal intensifier to emphasize a statement, often not literally true.
ex: The quiz was literally so hard that many students studied all night.
Her explanation was literally so clear that everyone understood.

s.defn: Interjection used to affirm that a statement is true in its most literal sense, signaling emphasis on factual accuracy in discussion, especially in educational contexts.
ex: Literally, the chart shows a straight line.
Literally, the data confirm the hypothesis.

s.defn: Interjection used to express strong emotion or surprise, often in casual speech, sometimes to emphasize a point or reaction, and can be hyperbolic.
ex: Literally, I could not believe the score.
Literally, this is the easiest problem we've seen.

s.defn: The act of coming to rest on the ground after flight; the moment of touchdown.
ex: The plane completed a smooth landing after the storm.
Pilots train to perform a safe landing in windy conditions.

s.defn: A flat platform between flights of stairs; a resting or turning place in a staircase.
ex: The staircase has a wide landing between flights.
Decorative plants sit on the stair landing.

s.defn: A place where boats land or dock, such as a shore or quay.
ex: The ship tied at the river landing near the market.
Fishermen hauled nets ashore at the landing.

s.defn: The act of obtaining something desirable, such as a job or contract.
ex: She landed a scholarship after months of auditions.
The company hopes to land a major contract this quarter.

s.defn: To bring something that is in the air or water to rest on a surface, typically a plane or bird.
ex: The plane is landing on the runway as scheduled.
A flock of birds landed softly on the treetop after the storm.

s.defn: To arrive at a place after traveling from another location.
ex: The ship landed at the port after a long voyage.
The hikers landed in the valley just before sunset.

s.defn: To obtain or secure something valuable through effort or luck, as in a job, deal, or scholarship.
ex: She landed a scholarship after winning the science fair.
The company landed a government contract after negotiations.

s.defn: Relating to the act of landing a vehicle, especially an aircraft or spacecraft; used to describe equipment, procedures, or sites involved in landing.
ex: The landing gear must deploy correctly during the landing sequence.
Students study the landing procedure in the aviation unit.

s.defn: A contract is a written or spoken agreement between two or more parties that creates legally binding obligations.
ex: The contract requires the seller to deliver books by the agreed date.
Students study how a contract states payment and responsibilities.

s.defn: The contract is the written record that documents the agreement including terms, dates, and signatures.
ex: The teacher asks learners to annotate the contract for key clauses.
A written contract serves as a reliable record of obligations.

s.defn: A social or informal contract is a promise or understanding that guides behavior but is not legally binding.
ex: In class, students may create an informal contract to share work.
The group signed a handshake agreement to publish results fairly.

s.defn: To enter into a legally binding agreement with another person or group.
ex: Families sign a contract before the field trip.
The school will execute a contract with the publisher for materials.

s.defn: To shrink in size, amount, or volume.
ex: When metal cools, it contracts and becomes smaller.
In dry air objects contract and reduce their volume.

s.defn: To catch and become infected with a disease.
ex: During winter, students may contract influenza after exposure.
If not careful, you can contract measles from an unvaccinated person.

s.defn: Concessive adverb used to introduce a counterpoint or qualification that follows a previous claim, roughly equivalent to nonetheless or in spite of that.
ex: The results were statistically significant nevertheless the effect size was small
The hypothesis held under initial testing nevertheless limitations include sample bias

s.defn: A strenuous effort to overcome a challenge or achieve a goal.
ex: The students faced a struggle to finish the long reading assignment.
Her struggle to master fractions lasted several weeks.

s.defn: A difficult situation or hardship that tests one's resources.
ex: The family faced a financial struggle after job loss.
Students often experience a daily struggle to stay organized.

s.defn: A violent or forceful fight or confrontation between people.
ex: The struggle between rival groups erupted at the stadium.
The struggle for independence involved many battles.

s.defn: To make a great effort to achieve something or to overcome a difficulty.
ex: The student struggled to balance the algebraic equations.
The scientists struggled to interpret the data.

Researchers noted the unity of the system during the experiment.

Community leaders called for unity after the incident.

s.defn: Relating to using resources in a way that does not harm the environment.

s.defn: A strong feeling of happiness or pleasure.

The joy of discovery motivates students to keep exploring.

Laughter filled the room as students shared joy during the celebration.

s.defn: A basic structure that supports and organizes a system or idea.

There are risks beside the potential benefits.

s.defn: A weight of type used to render text in bold for emphasis in writing and publishing.

A bold move showed willingness to risk.

s.defn: Confident and fearless in action or speech; not hesitant.

Her bold presentation impressed the panel.

Her outfit featured a bold red scarf.

The teacher asked students to bold the headings to organize the pages.

s.defn: To act with courage or to take a bold risk in a situation.

The team bolded the plan and presented a novel solution.

s.defn: To provide someone with the necessary items or equipment for a task or activity.

s.defn: To furnish a space or place with equipment or facilities; to outfit a room or facility.

The gym is equipped with modern machines.

s.defn: The act or process of guarding against harm or loss to keep someone or something safe from damage or danger.

A smoke detector provides protection by warning of fire.

Teachers ensure students have legal protection when reporting harassment to staff.

s.defn: The audible component of a multimedia signal that can be perceived by listeners, comprising speech, music, and other sounds, as distinct from visual content.

ex: The course covers audio engineering principles and practice.
Advances in audio processing improve speech intelligibility in mobile devices.

s.defn: Relating to sound, hearing, or the audible, especially as used in scientific or technical contexts.

Participants were exposed to audio stimuli presented via headphones.

s.defn: Relating to equipment, media, and processes that produce, transmit, or reproduce sound, including hardware and software components used in audio workflows.
ex: The lab compared audio interfaces and signal chains.
Software tools enable high fidelity audio processing for experiments.

s.defn: A small round mark made by a pen, pencil, stamp, or other instrument on a surface.

Samples were incubated overnight before measurement.

Prices rose overnight following the announcement.

s.defn: Happening or completed within a single night; rapid and often unexpected.

s.defn: A stay of one night at a hotel, dormitory, or other lodging; the act of staying overnight.

s.defn: The central business district of a city, where many offices and commercial activities are concentrated.

Residents enjoy living in downtown because of access to shops and transit.

s.defn: Located in or describing the central part of a city, especially the area with offices, shops, and government buildings.

Our field trip walked through downtown streets near city hall.

s.defn: Relating to or located in the central part of a town or city as a descriptor used in phrases like downtown campus or downtown offices.

Downtown offices faced the main square.

s.defn: Adverb meaning toward or into the central part of a city, typically used when talking about travel or movement.

The festival downtown attracted families.

s.defn: Genuine and honest in expression or intention; not feigned or deceptive.

s.defn: Expressed or communicated in a manner that conveys genuine emotion or commitment; not superficial.

s.defn: A thing or component that is placed into another object, often detachable, to complete or extend it.

The workbook came with a coupon insert for supplies.
